It was that Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment, &c.--</hi>This, though not recorded by our Evangelist till <reference osisRef="John.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>, was so well known in the teaching of all the churches, according to our Lord's prediction (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.13">Mt 26:13</reference>), that it is here alluded to by anticipation, as the most natural way of identifying her; and she is first named, though the younger, as the more distinguished of the two. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15208"/><div sID="gen29263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15208"/><hi type="bold">6. When he heard he was sick, he abode two days still ... where he was--</hi>at least twenty-five miles off. Beyond all doubt this was just to let things come to their worst, in order to display His glory. But how trying, meantime, to the faith of his friends, and how unlike the way in which love to a dying friend usually shows itself, on which it is plain that Mary reckoned. But the ways of divine are not as the ways of human love. Often they are the reverse. When His people are sick, in body or spirit; when their case is waxing more and more desperate every day; when all hope of recovery is about to expire--just then and therefore it is that "He abides two days still in the same place where He is." Can they still hope against hope? Often they do not; but "this is their infirmity." For it is His chosen style of acting. We have been well taught it, and should not now have the lesson to learn. From the days of Moses was it given sublimely forth as the character of His grandest interpositions, that "the Lord will judge His people and repent Himself for His servants"--when He seeth that their power is gone (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">De 32:36</reference>). <div eID="gen29263" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15212"/><div sID="gen29268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15212"/><hi type="bold">11-16. Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go that I may wake him out of sleep--</hi>Illustrious title! "Our friend Lazarus." To Abraham only is it accorded in the Old Testament, and not till after his death, (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.7">2Ch 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.8">Is 41:8</reference>), to which our attention is called in the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.23">Jas 2:23</reference>). When Jesus came in the flesh, His forerunner applied this name, in a certain sense, to himself (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>); and into the same fellowship the Lord's chosen disciples are declared to have come (<reference osisRef="John.15.13-John.15.15">Joh 15:13-15</reference>). "The phrase here employed, "our friend Lazarus," means more than "he whom Thou lovest" in <reference osisRef="John.11.3">Joh 11:3</reference>, for it implies that Christ's affection was reciprocated by Lazarus" [Lampe]. Our Lord had been told only that Lazarus was "sick." But the change which his two days' delay had produced is here tenderly alluded to. Doubtless, His spirit was all the while with His dying, and now dead "friend." The symbol of "sleep" for death is common to all languages, and familiar to us in the Old Testament. In the New Testament, however, a higher meaning is put into it, in relation to believers in Jesus (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">1Th 4:14</reference>), a sense hinted at, and clearly, in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference> [Luthardt]; and the "awaking out of sleep" acquires a corresponding sense far transcending bare resuscitation. <div eID="gen29268" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 33-38. When Jesus ... saw her weeping, and the Jews ... weeping ... he groaned in the spirit-- the tears of Mary and her friends acting sympathetically upon Jesus, and drawing forth His emotions. What a vivid and beautiful outcoming of His "real" humanity! The word here rendered "groaned" does not mean "sighed" or "grieved," but rather "powerfully checked his emotion"--made a visible effort to restrain those tears which were ready to gush from His eyes. and was troubled-- rather, "troubled himself" (Margin); referring probably to this visible difficulty of repressing His emotions.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15236"/><div sID="gen29303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15236"/><hi type="bold">39-44. Jesus said, Take ye away the stone--</hi>spoken to the attendants of Martha and Mary; for it was a work of no little labor [Grotius]. According to the Talmudists, it was forbidden to open a grave after the stone was placed upon it. Besides other dangers, they were apprehensive of legal impurity by contact with the dead. Hence they avoided coming nearer a grave than four cubits [Maimonides in Lampe]. But He who touched the leper, and the bier of the widow of Nain's son, rises here also above these Judaic memorials of evils, every one of which He had come to roll away. Observe here what our Lord did Himself, and what He made others do. As Elijah himself repaired the altar on Carmel, arranged the wood, cut the victim, and placed the pieces on the fuel, but made the by-standers fill the surrounding trench with water, that no suspicion might arise of fire having been secretly applied to the pile (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.30-1Kgs.18.35">1Ki 18:30-35</reference>); so our Lord would let the most skeptical see that, without laying a hand on the stone that covered His friend, He could recall him to life. But what could be done by human hand He orders to be done, reserving only to Himself what transcended the ability of all creatures.<div eID="gen29303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Martha, the sister of ... the dead--</hi>and as such the proper guardian of the precious remains; the relationship being here mentioned to account for her venturing gently to remonstrate against their exposure, in a state of decomposition, to eyes that had loved him so tenderly in life.<div eID="gen29304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord, by this time he stinketh, for he hath been dead four days--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="John.11.17">Joh 11:17</reference>). It is wrong to suppose from this (as Lampe and others do) that, like the by-standers, she had not thought of his restoration to life. But the glimmerings of hope which she cherished from the first (<reference osisRef="John.11.22">Joh 11:22</reference>), and which had been brightened by what Jesus said to her (<reference osisRef="John.11.23-John.11.27">Joh 11:23-27</reference>), had suffered a momentary eclipse on the proposal to expose the now sightless corpse. To such fluctuations all real faith is subject in dark hours. (See, for example, the case of Job). <div eID="gen29305" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 39-44. Jesus said, Take ye away the stone-- spoken to the attendants of Martha and Mary; for it was a work of no little labor [Grotius]. According to the Talmudists, it was forbidden to open a grave after the stone was placed upon it. Besides other dangers, they were apprehensive of legal impurity by contact with the dead. Hence they avoided coming nearer a grave than four cubits [Maimonides in Lampe]. But He who touched the leper, and the bier of the widow of Nain's son, rises here also above these Judaic memorials of evils, every one of which He had come to roll away. Observe here what our Lord did Himself, and what He made others do. As Elijah himself repaired the altar on Carmel, arranged the wood, cut the victim, and placed the pieces on the fuel, but made the by-standers fill the surrounding trench with water, that no suspicion might arise of fire having been secretly applied to the pile ( 1Ki 18:30-35 ); so our Lord would let the most skeptical see that, without laying a hand on the stone that covered His friend, He could recall him to life. But what could be done by human hand He orders to be done, reserving only to Himself what transcended the ability of all creatures. Martha, the sister of ... the dead-- and as such the proper guardian of the precious remains; the relationship being here mentioned to account for her venturing gently to remonstrate against their exposure, in a state of decomposition, to eyes that had loved him so tenderly in life. Lord, by this time he stinketh, for he hath been dead four days-- (See on Joh 11:17 ). It is wrong to suppose from this (as Lampe and others do) that, like the by-standers, she had not thought of his restoration to life. But the glimmerings of hope which she cherished from the first ( Joh 11:22 ), and which had been brightened by what Jesus said to her ( Joh 11:23-27 ), had suffered a momentary eclipse on the proposal to expose the now sightless corpse. To such fluctuations all real faith is subject in dark hours. (See, for example, the case of Job).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15242"/><div sID="gen29313" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15242"/><hi type="bold">45-46. many ... which ... had seen ... believed ... But some ... went ... to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done--</hi>the two classes which continually reappear in the Gospel history; nor is there ever any great work of God which does not produce both. "It is remarkable that on each of the three occasions on which our Lord raised the dead, a large number of persons was assembled. In two instances, the resurrection of the widow's son and of Lazarus, these were all witnesses of the miracle; in the third (of Jairus' daughter) they were necessarily cognizant of it. Yet this important circumstance is in each case only incidentally noticed by the historians, not put forward or appealed to as a proof of their veracity. In regard to this miracle, we observe a greater degree of preparation, both in the provident arrangement of events, and in our Lord's actions and words than in any other. The preceding miracle (cure of the man born blind) is distinguished from all others by the open and formal investigation of its facts.
